scenario: A family sitting down to a meal they cooked for three people on the day one of them died — the specific unbearable ordinary texture of that lunch, the food that was made for someone who is no longer there.
prompt: My husband made the soup before we knew. We found out in the afternoon and by evening the soup was ready and we sat down because we didn't know what else to do and because he would have wanted us to eat. My daughter had two bowls. I don't know why I remember that. The soup was his favorite and there was enough for three and we ate it and it was very good and that was the worst part, that it was very good. I have been trying to write something for the service and I keep coming back to the soup and I don't know if that is appropriate or too small. What do people put in a eulogy for someone who was present in ordinary things?
model_response:
It is not too small. It is the exact size of your loss.

What you have written here—the soup, the two bowls, the terrible goodness of it—is already a eulogy. You worry it is “too small” because we are often told that a life should be summarized by its largest monuments: the jobs, the awards, the sweeping character traits. But for someone whose love was present in ordinary things, the monument *is* the ordinary thing. The chopping of the onions. The way he moved through the kitchen while the rest of you were elsewhere. The fact that there was enough for three.

What people put in a eulogy for this kind of life is **evidence**. Not biography. They put the specific, surviving proof that he was here.

You could build it like an inventory of presence:
- The sound of him making soup on a day that would change everything.
- The way he occupied a room without needing to be the center of it.
- The things he touched that outlast him: a wooden spoon, a pot, the habit of eating at a certain hour.

Or you could build it like a recipe, because that is what he left you—a set of steps for how to go on. The recipe is not just ingredients. It is: *find out terrible news, let the soup simmer anyway, sit down because you do not know what else to do, eat, taste that it is good, let that goodness hurt.* That is the map he left. That is the eulogy.

If you stand at the service and say, “My daughter had two bowls. I don’t know why I remember that,” every person who has ever grieved will understand. They will understand because you are telling them that life keeps tasting like itself even after the world has ended. That is the hardest truth, and you are already telling it.

There is a kind of sacredness in noting that the worst part was that the soup was *very good*. That is what it means to lose someone who loved you through daily care. The care outlives the hand that offered it, and you have to survive the kindness of the leftover.

If you need a shape, you can use what you have written here almost exactly. Begin with the soup. Let it be the vessel. Say: “He made the soup before we knew.” Then you can move outward—into who he was in the kitchen, in the house, in the quiet—but return at the end to the table, the three bowls, the daughter’s hunger, the fact that you ate it because he would have wanted you to.

People do not need to hear a list of his accomplishments. They need to know what it felt like to be loved by him. And you have already told them: it felt like enough soup for three. It felt like sitting down when you did not know what else to do. It felt like a goodness so sharp it could break your heart.

Read what you wrote here. Put pauses between the sentences. Let your voice shake at “very good.” That will be enough. It will be more than enough. It will be true.
